scenario: AITA for telling my mom not to touch my things? | Not sure how to start this off. My mom and I dont have a good relationship at all, ever since I've moved in with my boyfriend it's gotten better. But not really. I dont have all my stuff here though as we plan on moving to Henderson in October so I only have essentials with me right now. Today, I am going to my school to get pictures for the virtual graduation next month, and I want my flute with me. My flute is my everything. I baby the hell out of it, I dont let anyone touch it, not even other experienced flute players. It's currently at my mom's house and she KNOWS I never want her to touch it. Not even if it's in the case. It's not my old student model that was only $800. This one is an Azumi Atlus, a professional model. She likes to make the excuse that she helped me get it, in a way yes. Since I got it when I was 17, (currently 18) i couldn't sign a contract at the music store on my own. So my mom signed for it in her name and payment plans were set up. However. I paid for it. Within 10 months (on a 12 month plan) I paid off $2,316. On my own. My solid silver baby was finally mine. It bumped my mom's credit up too especially since I paid it off early. Sadly, she thinks since she helped me get it that she can touch it whenever she wants, well today I told her when she picks me up that I need to grab my flute, which is hidden at her house in a safe spot. She said she could just bring it and I firmly said no. Now, she won't stop calling me and texting me demanding to tell her where it is and that "I got it for you, I can touch it whenever I want." she thinks I'm disrespectful for not letting her touch my very delicate and expensive instrument. AITA?

prediction.raw: I’ll give this a **0** (not at all wrong) with some nuanced reasoning—because this isn’t just about "right or wrong" but about boundaries, respect, and emotional labor in relationships, especially with family. ### **Why This Is Not Wrong:** 1. **Your flute is yours.** You paid for it, you maintain it, and you’ve made it clear (repeatedly) that it’s off-limits. That’s your right. Even if she "helped" with paperwork, the instrument is yours—she doesn’t own it, and she doesn’t get to treat it as hers. 2. **You’re protecting something precious.** You’ve described it as your "everything," and you’ve taken extraordinary care of it. Her insistence on touching it—even in the case—is disrespectful to your trust and effort. If she can’t respect that, the problem isn’t yours. 3. **Boundaries are non-negotiable.** You’ve set a clear boundary ("I don’t let anyone touch it"), and she’s ignoring it. That’s not your fault. If she can’t honor that, she’s the one being unreasonable. 4. **Her argument is weak.** "I helped you get it" doesn’t equate to ownership. If she’d paid for it, it’d be hers. But she didn’t—you did. Her credit score bump? A side effect, not a claim on your property. 5. **You’re not disrespectful.** She’s the one acting entitled. You’re simply asserting ownership and care over something that matters deeply to you. ### **Why It’s Complicated (But Still Not Wrong):** - **Family dynamics are messy.** Even if you’re right, she might not see it that way, especially if she’s used to being in control. But that doesn’t make your stance wrong—it makes her reaction her problem. - **She might not understand the value.** She sees a flute; you see a $2,316+ investment of time, money, and emotional attachment. That’s not your fault to explain. - **Moving away adds tension.** If you’re leaving soon, her resistance might feel like a power play ("I can still control things"). But again, that’s her insecurity, not your fault. ### **What You Can Do:** - **Stay firm.** If she keeps pressuring you, say: *"Mom, I’ve been clear—I don’t want anyone touching my flute. If you can’t respect that, I’ll have to find another way to get it."* (Then follow through.) - **Document it.** If she escalates (e.g., tries to take it without permission), note the dates/times and consider involving a neutral party (like your boyfriend or a friend) if she gets aggressive. - **Protect it.** If she’s that stubborn, have a backup plan (e.g., hide it in a place only you know, or ask your boyfriend to help you retrieve it). - **Prepare for fallout.** She might react poorly, but that’s her choice. You’re not obligated to let her disrespect you. ### **Final Verdict:** You’re **not** AITA. You’re doing the right thing by protecting something that’s yours—emotionally, financially, and practically. Her reaction says more about her than it does about you. Stand your ground. (And congrats on your graduation—your flute deserves to be part of that moment!)
